History Timeline
Olongapo City
From Gently Sloping Shore to Smart City
Pre-Colonial → Present
🏹
Before 1500s
Aeta Ancestral Domain
The Gently Sloping Shore
Long before colonial intervention, the area was the ancestral domain of the Aeta people. In the Sambal language, the region was called 'olang-gapo' — meaning a 'gently sloping shore,' describing the natural coastal landscape.
📌 Did You Know?
The Legend of Ulo ng Apo: A wise chieftain named Apo led the village with fairness and justice. Rival tribes abducted and beheaded him. When his head was found impaled on a bamboo pole, the villagers did not flee — they cried 'Ulo ng Apo!' as a rallying call for unity. This spirit of unity remains central to Olongapo's identity today.
⚓
1884 – 1898
Arsenal de Olongapo
Spain's Pacific Stronghold
In 1884, King Alfonso XII declared Subic Bay as Spain's primary naval stronghold. Construction of the Arsenal de Olongapo began on March 8, 1885. Engineers dredged the harbor and built a drainage canal that turned the naval station into an island for defense.
📌 Did You Know?
The Spanish Gate (West Gate), built in 1885, remains the ONLY surviving 19th-century remnant of this era. It served as the arsenal's main entrance and later as a jail. It was declared a historical landmark in 2013.
🦅
1899 – 1941
US Naval Reservation
Roosevelt's Pacific Base
American Colonial Era
On December 10, 1899, the first American flag was raised at Olongapo. President Theodore Roosevelt established the Subic Bay Naval Reservation in 1901, placing the civilian community under direct U.S. Navy jurisdiction. Massive quarrying caused Kalalake hill to disappear entirely — leaving a lagoon now part of Bicentennial Park.
📌 Did You Know?
Unlike the rest of the Philippines, Olongapo residents paid taxes directly to the U.S. Navy, and the base commander served as chairman of the town council.
🔥
1941 – 1945
Scorched Earth & Liberation
Twice Burned, Never Broken
On December 13, 1941, Japanese air raids killed 12 civilians in Olongapo. On December 24, residents burned the entire town to the ground to deny resources to advancing Japanese forces. The Japanese occupied the ruins from January 10, 1942 until early 1945.
📌 Did You Know?
Olongapo was burned TWICE — once by its own people to resist the Japanese, and again by retreating Japanese forces before liberation in 1945. After the war, the town was rebuilt on a new site north of its original location.
🇵🇭
1946 – 1966
Return to Filipino Hands
From Navy Town to City
Sovereignty & Cityhood
After 1946, Olongapo remained under U.S. Navy control while the rest of the Philippines was independent. Tensions peaked in 1959 after the killing of local businessman Robert Grant by an American sentry. On December 7, 1959, the town was finally surrendered to the Philippine government.
📌 Did You Know?
Olongapo was chartered as a city on June 1, 1966 — and declared a Highly Urbanized City on December 7, 1983.
🌃
1960s – 1970s
Sin City of the Philippines
R&R Capital of the Pacific Fleet
Vietnam War R&R Era
In the 1960s and 70s, Olongapo became the primary Rest & Recreation destination for the U.S. Seventh Fleet during the Vietnam War. Magsaysay Drive overflowed with bars, nightclubs, and restaurants — earning the city the nickname 'Sin City of the Philippines.'
📌 Did You Know?
At its peak, the base employed over 42,000 Filipino workers. The Fil-Am Club House, Club Enterprise, Galaxy Nite Club — these were the landmarks of a city that never slept.
🎶
1960s – 1970s
Magsaysay Drive
The Street That Never Slept
Vietnam War Strip
Club Enterprise and Galaxy Nite Club were landmarks of Magsaysay Drive — the commercial heart of old Olongapo. American sailors and Filipino workers filled the street day and night. The famous 'Cubi Cat' at NAS Cubi Point Officers' Club — a catapult ride built in 1969 — became legend among aviators.
📌 Did You Know?
The 'Cubi Cat' was a 6-foot vehicle shaped like an A-7 Corsair II. Pilots were catapulted across the officers' club — those who missed the 'arresting wire' landed in a 3.5-foot pool of water!
🏙️
1980s
Model City Transformation
Mayor Richard Gordon's Legacy
Gordon Era
Mayor Richard Gordon transformed Olongapo in the 1980s into one of the most progressive and crime-free cities in the Philippines. Clean streets, strict civic discipline, and economic management made Olongapo a national model of urban governance.
📌 Did You Know?
Gordon's philosophy: 'There are no bad places, only bad leaders.' Olongapo under Gordon was frequently cited as the best-managed city in the Philippines — a stark contrast to its 'Sin City' reputation just a decade earlier.
🌋
1991 – 1992
The End of an Era
Ash, Votes & Departure
Mt. Pinatubo & Base Closure
On June 15, 1991, Mount Pinatubo erupted catastrophically. Olongapo was buried under a foot of wet ash — roofs collapsed across the city, killing over 60 people. In the wake of this disaster, the Philippine Senate voted to reject renewal of the Military Bases Agreement.
📌 Did You Know?
November 24, 1992: The last U.S. Navy ship departed Subic Bay. Under Mayor Richard Gordon and 8,000 unpaid volunteers, BILLIONS of dollars in property were protected from looting — the 'Miracle of Volunteerism' that made the SBMA possible.
🌏
1992 – Present
Subic Bay Freeport Zone
From Naval Base to Global Hub
Under Republic Act 7227, the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority (SBMA) transformed 14,000 hectares of former naval base into a world-class economic freeport. Today SBMA hosts 800+ companies — from Ocean Adventure and Zoobic Safari to FedEx's Asian hub and international shipping giants.
📌 Did You Know?
The SBMA transformation is considered one of the most successful military-to-civilian base conversions in the world. The SALIN-LAHI project — as part of the DOST Smart City program — continues this legacy of transformation through digital heritage preservation.
